Networked Seamless

One computer keeps the data and the others connect to it - the Server and its Clients, the relay, pairing, approvals from any browser, and what stops when the Server is out of reach.

On this page
  • Three kinds of computer
  • How a Client reaches the Server
  • The relay
  • Pairing
  • Revocation
  • Locked projects across computers
  • Approvals from any browser
  • When the Server is out of reach
  • Related

Seamless is Standalone by default: the daemon, the data and the agents that use them, all on one computer. Networked is the other shape. One computer, the Server, keeps the data, and every other computer is a Client of it, so a laptop, a desktop and a build box share one corpus instead of three that drift apart. seamlessd setup, which the installer runs before it installs anything, asks which a computer will be.

This page is the model. Share one daemon across your computers has the steps.

Three kinds of computer

Standalone Networked: Server Networked: Client
In setup's words everything on this computer: the daemon, the data, and the agents that use them this computer keeps the data, and the other computers connect to it this computer connects to the Server and keeps no data of its own
The daemon runs here runs here none: seamlessd serve refuses on a client
The data here here, for every computer none; it is the Server's
Its agents reach this daemon this daemon the Server, through a relay or with a key
Offered on macOS, Linux, Windows macOS, Linux macOS, Linux, Windows

Set up the Server first: every Client needs its address. A Client never starts from a backup, since its data is the Server's. A Standalone install can become the Server later. Setup does not make a computer that keeps its own data a Client, or a Client anything else: those moves are by hand.

Windows is never the Server. Setup offers it Standalone and Client only, and says why: "Windows has no peer_auth and no relay, so a Windows computer can be a Client but not the Server". A Windows Client is always a key client: it never runs the relay, and its agents never open a locked project.

How a Client reaches the Server

There are two ways, and the difference is what the Server can tell apart.

  • Through a relay (macOS and Linux). The relay is a small daemon on the Client, run by an account of its own. Agents dial a local socket, exactly as they would beside a peer_auth daemon, and the computer holds no bearer key. The Server learns each request's local account and process chain, as its own socket does.
  • With a key (Windows, and a computer where you have no root, such as a container or CI). The Client's config holds a key of its own, from its pairing, and dials the Server's address. The Server sees one caller: you, as the bearer key is.
Through a relay With a key
Platforms macOS, Linux any; Windows always
Root on the Client to install the relay none
What the Client holds the relay's private key, readable by its account alone its own key in your config (0600)
What the Server learns of a caller its uid and process chain, believed under peer_auth for a relay you map nothing: every request is you
Locked projects judged per agent, for a relay you map under peer_auth (below) never

Setup pairs a macOS or Linux Client as a relay unless you ask for a key, and Windows always as a key device. A Client can still use the Server's own key instead, which seamlessd client-config prints on the Server: that pairs nothing, and the Devices page does not list it.

The relay

seamlessd relay is the same binary, run on the Client as a system account of its own. It serves the socket agents dial beside a peer_auth daemon, /opt/seamless/run/seamlessd.sock, so seam, its hooks, the seam mcp-proxy bridge and the Touch ID helper reach the Server through it exactly as they reach a daemon on their own computer. For each local connection it reads the caller's uid and process chain from its own kernel, and forwards the request to the Server over TLS with its own client certificate, carrying those two facts. It runs on macOS and Linux only, the platforms whose kernels name a socket's peer.

Why it needs root. The uid and chain it reports are believed only because no process of yours can change what the relay says. So it runs as an account of its own, pinned by root as the daemon's account is on a peer_auth server, with its files where only that account and root can write: the binary, the socket's directory, and its data directory, /opt/seamless/relay (0700), which holds its private key. It refuses to run as root or as your account, and refuses any layout another account could change. Root sets up the account and that layout; the relay itself never runs as root.

What it sees. The uid and process chain of each local caller, and every request and answer it forwards: it is a proxy, so whatever an agent behind it reads passes through it. It reads none of your files. What a hook captures from the agent's files, seam hook reads as you, beside the agent.

What it never does: decide. The Server judges every request. The relay says who is asking, never that you said yes. It interprets no content, caches nothing and answers nothing from memory, and it forwards only to the certificate the Server presented when the relay paired.

What the Server trusts it for. Under peer_auth the Server judges a relay only once you map it in peer_auth.relays, and refuses it until then. Through a mapped relay your uid there is you, a restricted account you list there is that account, labeled with the computer's name, and any other uid is refused (how). Root, or the relay's account, on the Client can report any uid and chain, so every lease is keyed on the relay: a forged report reaches only what that relay's agents were approved. Without peer_auth on the Server, every request a relay forwards is you, whatever uid it names, so the socket's mode and group are the only gate on that computer. Setup's root step hands the socket to a group of you and the relay alone (mode 0660); seamlessd doctor on the Client warns when every local account may connect (relay.access).

Pairing

A computer pairs with the Server once, with a one-time code you get on the Server, and from then on holds a credential of its own, which you can revoke: a relay, a TLS certificate over its own key; a key device, a key of its own. A Client that uses the Server's own key has not paired.

  • The code. Get a pairing code on the console's Devices page, or seamlessd devices code on the Server. A code works once, for 10 minutes and for one computer; only its hash is stored, and at most 16 wait at once.
  • Without peer_auth, the code is the approval: whoever enters it first pairs as you. Use it on your own computer, and get a new one for each computer.
  • Under peer_auth, the code alone pairs nothing. The computer waits, for up to 10 minutes, until you approve it with your passkey on the Devices page, after checking that the fingerprint there is the one that computer shows.
  • Two fingerprints. The Server's certificate fingerprint (its SHA-256, as openssl x509 -noout -fingerprint -sha256 prints it): the Client shows it before it sends the code, for you to compare with the one the Server printed, and a relay pins that certificate from then on. A certificate the Client's own roots do not trust is trusted only once compared, and then as that certificate alone. The relay's key fingerprint: the relay prints it, and the Devices page shows it for your approval.
  • A paired computer speaks for its name. The name it paired with, its host name by default, is the host every request of it is recorded under, whatever the request says. No two live devices share a name, and none takes the Server's own.
  • A paired computer is you, at most. A key device reaches what the bearer key reaches. A relay does too without peer_auth; under it, the Server judges a relay you map as its own socket judges a request, and refuses one you have not mapped.

A relay needs TLS on the daemon's own listener. It proves itself with a client certificate in the TLS handshake, so a proxy that ends TLS in front of the daemon lets key devices pair but not relays.

Pairing is on only on a Server that serves other computers: TLS, a bind beyond loopback, or a server_url naming another host. A default install has no Devices page and no pairing endpoint, and asks no browser for a certificate.

Revocation

Revoke a computer on the Devices page, or with seamlessd devices revoke <id|name> on the Server. Its credential is refused from its next request, and the requests it is making end: at once from the page, within 30 seconds from the terminal. A relay's leases, read grants and waiting access requests end in the same step. A pairing that waits is denied instead.

A revoked computer pairs again with a new code. A relay pairs again with seamlessd relay pair --replace, after you revoke its old pairing: the Server refuses a second live device of the same name.

Locked projects across computers

A locked project opens only to an agent whose process tree holds a lease you approved, and only a kernel can name that tree.

  • Agents on the Server's own computer, on its peer_auth socket, open a locked project as Lock projects behind your approval describes.
  • Agents behind a relay peer_auth.relays maps are judged as that socket judges them. The relay names the program of every process it forwards, so an agent there asks for access as it would on the Server: never a shell, terminal or multiplexer, only an agent program or a process an agent started. Every approval shows a relay warning naming the computer whose pid, uid and program they are, and the lease is keyed on the relay and the process. A relay from before program names files nothing: update Seamless on that computer.
  • Key devices, key clients of the Server's own key, and the bearer key never hold a lease, so they never open a locked project. A Windows computer is always one of these. A relay you do not map gets nothing at all.

So run agents that need a locked project on the Server's computer, or behind a relay the Server maps.

Approvals from any browser

Every passkey approval in the console is a ceremony the Server verifies, whichever computer the browser runs on: an agent's access request, a console unlock, a lock change, a device pairing under peer_auth, and a restore while a project is locked. The browser must be signed in to the console, on the Server's passkey origin: the https address of the Server's name.

Under peer_auth, terminal approvals run only on the Server's computer, in a terminal there or over SSH to it: seam approve, seamlessd approve, the code a console unlock shows (seamlessd console-open --unlock), and every seamlessd approvers verb. Each proves itself by becoming the daemon's account, which exists only on the Server; a Client's relay never vouches that you said yes.

A browser on a Client signs in to the Server's console with the key, or with a passkey under console.sign_in: passkey, so that no browser needs the key (how).

When the Server is out of reach

A Client keeps no data of its own, so nothing on it works without the Server.

  • Through a relay, every request is refused at once, with the reason. The relay answers 502 and seamless relay: the server at <address> could not be reached (...); nothing is answered from memory, so every call fails until it answers. A Server that presents another certificate than the one the relay pinned gets the same kind of refusal, naming the fix. The relay starts even while the Server is down, and forwards again as soon as it answers.
  • With a key, the connection fails.
  • Either way, the hooks fail open. A session starts with no briefing, and what its hooks would have sent is lost: nothing is queued for later. MCP tools and seam commands fail with the reason.

A renewed certificate is a new certificate. A relay pins the exact certificate the Server presented at pairing, so renewing it (a tailnet certificate lasts 90 days) refuses every relay until it pairs again. Troubleshooting has the fix.
